description: We are TerraNovaX26, a team passionate about AI, Machine Learning, and space exploration. Our mission is to identify Earth locations that resemble potential permanent Moon and Mars base sites. We aim to use scientific data analysis, visualization, and innovative technology to explore environmental similarities and support future space exploration.
summary:
We developed a bilingual (Arabic and English) web app that helps mission planners choose where on Earth to prepare for the Moon and Mars. Users pick a target, and the app compares ten Earth analog sites against it on terrain, geology, climate and operational relevance. It ranks the sites, shows the top three, and places every site on an interactive map. Each site also gets its own “Analog Passport”: a profile with its location, environment, key characteristics, similarities, limitations and possible field experiments. Charts compare temperature, rainfall, solar energy and similarity across sites.
This addresses the challenge of linking NASA’s planetary observations to practical preparation on Earth. Analog sites are usually chosen by experience and reputation, with no clear link to a specific lunar or Martian region.

It matters because testing rovers, habitats and crew procedures in the right environment saves cost and reduces mission risk. Every value is tied to its source, with links to NASA POWER, LOLA, the Planetary Data System and Earthdata, and the scoring method is shown openly.
That comes to about 175 words, inside the 50–200 range.
One point to check before you submit: the summary says every value is tied to its source, and the app links to those four NASA portals. details:
What it does and how it works
Analog Passport is a single-page web app. The user chooses the Moon or Mars, then a target region. The app compares ten Earth analog sites against that target using four similarity scores: terrain, geology, climate and operations. It combines them into one overall score, weighted 25%, 30%, 25% and 20%, and ranks the sites. Results can be filtered by country, environment and geology, and the full comparison table can be sorted. An interactive map shows every site, with different marker colors for Moon and Mars matches. Each site has an Analog Passport covering its coordinates, elevation, climate, terrain, geology, water and dust, planetary matches, advantages, limitations and possible field experiments. Five charts compare temperature, rainfall, solar energy, similarity and the overall ranking.

Benefits and intended impact
It gives mission planners and students a clear, transparent way to choose where to test equipment and train crews. Showing the formula and the weights lets users see why a site ranks where it does. The goal is better-prepared missions at lower cost and risk.

Tools and technology
HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for the map and Chart.js for the charts. Fonts are IBM Plex Sans Arabic and Space Grotesk. The data is a JSON dataset, and the app runs entirely in the browser. We used Claude, an AI assistant, to help build the code.

Creativity
The “passport” idea turns each site into a travel document for a mission. The app is fully bilingual with right-to-left Arabic, and it uses a NASA-inspired dark space design.

Factors we considered
Transparency of scoring, accessibility in Arabic and English, a layout that works on desktop, tablet and phone, covering both the Moon and Mars, and listing each site’s limitations next to its strengths. We also linked the NASA sources used for verification.
